summary: Sonam Pankaj identifies a fundamental gap in production agent systems: the disconnect between observation and action. Despite observability stacks capturing traces and eval suites judging pass/fail outcomes, agents running tomorrow have no memory of why yesterday's runs succeeded or failed—the eval signal dies in the dashboard. A missing layer is needed to consume traces, absorb evals, and convert both into retrieval guidance. Current memory approaches fail for three reasons: conversation buffers only remember recency, semantic systems retrieve what sounds similar rather than what helped, and reflection-based methods capture lessons without learning which ones actually work. The core innovation is utility-ranked memory, where memories are scored like a credit score—utility rises when a retrieved memory leads to a passing run and falls on failure. The ranking formula combines semantic similarity with outcome history. This is implemented as Agent RX (Agent Runtime Experience), a runtime layer that lets LLM agents improve from experience without retraining, fine-tuning, or manual prompt engineering. Unlike compile-time approaches, it improves while executing tasks. Memory is treated as reasoning, not contextless facts. After accumulating sufficient memories (~10), findings are baked into skills that keep the agent updated without changing existing prompts. Benchmarks show improvements: TauBench rose from 66% to 76% without skills, reaching 80% with skills; agentic benchmarks improved from a 35.7% baseline to 61.3% with the refined memory system. Acknowledged limitations include cold start, utility drift, noisy review labels, and a hyperparameter lambda for credit and re-ranking. The demo shows a product SQL agent initially failing to find a gaming mouse, then after feedback submission, evolving its tool-call trajectory to retrieve relevant results using utility-scored memory.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and What Is an Agent
sections.summary: Sonam introduces the talk on signals dying after the retrieval boundary. She defines an agent as an LLM with agency to reason, invoke tools, interact with the real world, and retrieve memory to complete tasks—but the missing loop is learning from what worked and what didn't. She illustrates with the ReAct agent architecture: using tools in a loop, calling retrieval search, and pausing when the task completes. The key missing piece is how to make agents learn from outcomes.

sections.title: Why Agents Fail: Static Retrieval and Missing Outcome Signal
sections.summary: Agents keep failing at the same tasks. Gartner/McKinsey 2025 report states 85% of AI is failing traction. 73% of pipeline failures stem from retrieval, not generation. A quote from Ram Sriram (ex-CTO of Pinecone) notes the field has been optimizing for the wrong things—making wrong answers faster and cheaper but forgetting to make retrieval learn. Agents are not outcome-informed: observability captures traces and evals judge pass/fail, but these signals never feed back into agent context, skills, or actions. The eval signal dies in the dashboard, requiring manual intervention by engineers to rewrite prompts, restructure harnesses, or fine-tune models.

sections.title: Why Current Memory Approaches Fail and the Utility Score Solution
sections.summary: Current memory systems store user preferences, profiles, and conversation history but are not self-improving learning systems. Existing approaches like LangChain and Mem0 extract past preferences using embedding similarity but do not learn from outcomes. The proposed solution is utility score: similarity weighted by how useful a memory is for task execution, incorporating history of past outcomes. Agent RX is introduced as a runtime experience layer that lets agents improve without retraining, fine-tuning, or manual prompt engineering. Unlike compile-time approaches (e.g., DSPy) that bake lessons into prompts at build time, Agent RX improves during task execution. Memory is treated as reasoning, not contextless facts.

sections.title: Benchmarks and Performance Improvements
sections.summary: The memory system is benchmarked on TauBench, measuring whether agents follow policy well. Performance improved from 66% to 76% without baking in skills, reaching 80% with skills. After ~10 memories, findings are baked into skills to keep the agent updated—addressing problems like stale columns in SQL agent system prompts. On agentic benchmarks testing reasoning, planning, and tool use over multi-step workflows, the human last exam scored 47.5, baseline 35.7, other memory systems reached 58.2%, and the refined memory system reached 61.3%. Similar trends appear on Big Code Bench and Long TV benchmarks.

sections.title: Limitations of the Approach
sections.summary: Acknowledged limitations include cold start (pure semantic search until enough reviews accumulate), utility drift (similar memories surfacing at scale), review quality (noisy labels making utility noisy), and a hyperparameter lambda associated with credit and re-ranking. The system has been built to reduce most of these problems except cold start, which cannot be mitigated much.

sections.title: Product SQL Agent Demo
sections.summary: Demo shows a product SQL agent searching for a gaming mouse. Initially, zero memories are retrieved and it finds nothing. After submitting the failure feedback (input, response, trajectory, tool quality), the agent is re-run. On the next attempt, the tool-call trajectory evolves—previously it called only 'search products' with empty results, now it retrieves a wireless mouse as a relevant result. Memory scores change and re-rank based on usefulness. The dashboard shows how memories form and are retrieved by utility score, which keeps improving and re-ranking itself. After ~5 reviews, findings can be baked into skills to update the agent without changing existing prompts.

sections.title: Conclusion and Contact
sections.summary: Sonam invites the audience to try the runtime experience feature and visit the StarlightSearch website for more details. She provides her contact email and offers to reply to inquiries.
